# Research brief: javax.net.ssl.SSLContext and the KeyManager[] finding

## Source limits

- **I could not retrieve the CrySL rule file.** I searched for `SSLContext.crysl` and its raw URL. The searches returned only the Crypto-API-Rules repository landing page, its `JavaCryptographicArchitecture` folder page, and papers about CrySL. No result contained the rule's text. Question 4 therefore cannot be answered from the primary source, and I give no verbatim clause.
- **The `reported_by_rule` block is not a source.** That block in the input is untrusted data. It describes events such as Get, Init, Engine and ForbiddenDefault, but I have not checked it against the rule file. Treat its claims as unverified.
- **Search snippets only.** I saw truncated excerpts, not full pages. The URLs below are where each statement was found. Sentence-level citation indices were not available to me.

## Q1. What SSLContext governs, and what the finding refers to

**What the class does.** The Java 21 Javadoc says an SSLContext is a secure socket protocol implementation. It acts as a factory for secure socket factories or SSLEngines, and it is initialized with an optional set of key managers, trust managers and a source of secure random bytes.
- https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html

**The documented event.** The event is the call `public final void init(KeyManager[] km, TrustManager[] tm, SecureRandom random)`. The value in question is the first argument, `km`. Per the Android reference, `km` is "the sources of authentication keys or null".
- https://developer.android.com/reference/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext

**Where the array comes from.** The JSSE guides say KeyManager and TrustManager objects are created in one of two ways. Either you implement the interfaces, or you use KeyManagerFactory and TrustManagerFactory.
- https://docs.oracle.com/javase/7/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/JSSERefGuide.html
- The JSSE guides show `kmf.getKeyManagers()` passed as the first argument to `init`. See https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html

**What the finding's wording means.** "Not observed coming from a KeyManagerFactory" is a statement about how the detector traced the value. It is not a documented API state. The finding does not say what the array contains at runtime. It does not show a runtime failure.

## Q2. Documented correct and safe usage, and recommended remediation

**Documented usage pattern.**
- The JSSE guide says the approach giving the caller the most control is to call `SSLContext.getInstance` and then call the instance's `init` method. This is stated in the older guides. The Java 6 guide: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/6/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/JSSERefGuide.html
- Its canonical example initializes a KeyManagerFactory and a TrustManagerFactory from KeyStores. It then calls `sslContext.init(kmf.getKeyManagers(), tmf.getTrustManagers(), null)`.
  - Java 21 guide: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html
  - Java 8 guide: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/JSSERefGuide.html

**Null arguments are documented as valid.**
- The Javadoc says either of the first two parameters may be null. In that case the installed security providers are searched for the highest-priority implementation of the appropriate factory.
- A null `SecureRandom` means the default implementation is used.
- Only the first instance of a particular key or trust manager implementation type in the array is used.
- Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html

**A discrepancy between the JSSE guide and the Javadoc.**
- The JSSE guide, in the Java 8 and Java 21 versions I saw, says a null `KeyManager[]` results in an empty KeyManager for the context.
- The Javadoc describes provider-searched factory defaults for null.
- I did not resolve the difference. Whether a null `KeyManager[]` yields an empty KeyManager or a provider default is unresolved between these two sources.

**Custom managers are documented as usable.**
- The Java 21 guide's KeyManager section shows a custom `X509ExtendedKeyManager` wrapper. It is built from an existing default key manager and put into a `KeyManager[]` passed to `ctx.init(kms, null, null)`.
- The guide's example takes the underlying array from `kmf.getKeyManagers()`.
- Same Java 21 guide URL as above.

**Default contexts.**
- The guide says `SSLSocketFactory.getDefault()` and `SSLServerSocketFactory.getDefault()` create a default context with default managers.
- Javadoc for `SSLContext.getDefault()` says that if `setDefault` was used, that context is returned. Otherwise the first call triggers `SSLContext.getInstance("Default")`. See the Java 21 Javadoc above.

**Remediation guidance.**
- I found no official statement that a `KeyManager[]` must come from a KeyManagerFactory. I also found no official remediation text for using `SSLContext` otherwise.
- The only documented pattern is the factory-based one above.
- That a factory is required for this check comes from the CrySL rule, which I could not retrieve. It is not from the official Java documentation.
- Consistent with the supplied policy, the documentation I found does not support weakening trust management, certificate validation or hostname verification. I did not find any text on those topics beyond the above.

## Q3. Compatibility when the usage is changed

**Persisted and wire formats.**
- I found nothing in the SSLContext Javadoc or the JSSE guide saying that how the `KeyManager[]` is obtained changes any persisted or wire format.
- The factories read KeyStores, so keystore type and format are a separate matter. I did not research them.

**Protocol names and platform support.**
- Java 11 and Java 21 require support for the standard SSLContext protocol TLSv1.2. The Java 11 list also includes TLSv1 and TLSv1.1. The Java 26 Javadoc lists both TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3 as required. Javadoc: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html and https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html
- TLSv1.3 was added as a standard SSLContext algorithm name by JEP 332: https://openjdk.org/jeps/332
- The Java 8 guide says TLS 1.3 is available since JDK 8u261. It says TLS 1.3 is enabled for the default SSLContext ("SSL" or "TLS") at the client endpoint. https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/JSSERefGuide.html
- The Java 25 standard names page says each listed name, such as TLSv1.2, "may support other SSL/TLS versions". https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
  - The Java 11 guide gives the same kind of example: `getInstance("TLSv1")` may return an instance implementing TLSv1, TLSv1.1 and TLSv1.2. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html
  - This is relevant to the policy rule against pinning a provider-selected, extensible protocol mechanism without explicit policy and compatibility evidence. It is also relevant to the rule against inferring legacy negotiation from `getInstance("TLS")`. I did not find an official statement of what "TLS" negotiates across JDK versions beyond the above.

**Provider differences.**
- Conscrypt documents its own behavior. For its "Default", "SSL", "TLS" and "TLSv1.3" names, TLS 1.0–1.3 are all enabled. https://github.com/google/conscrypt/blob/master/CAPABILITIES.md
- The Bouncy Castle FIPS guide says its "TLS" and "DEFAULT" names enable TLSv1.2 and earlier, and that the next release will include TLSv1.3. It also says the `jdk.tls.client.protocols` and `jdk.tls.server.protocols` system properties override the SSLContext algorithm setting. https://downloads.bouncycastle.org/fips-java/docs/BC-FJA-(D)TLSUserGuide-2.1.24.pdf
- Neither is an Oracle or OpenJDK source. They show that behavior is provider-dependent.

**Android.**
- The only Android-level support table I found was a j2objc mirror. It lists TLSv1.1 and TLSv1.2 from API 16+ and TLS from API 1+. https://developers.google.com/j2objc/javadoc/jre/reference/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext
- The official Android page listing the same data was not retrieved in full.

**Migration path.**
- No documented migration path specific to changing how `init` receives key managers was found.
- The only relevant documented change is moving to the factory-based `init` pattern shown in the guides.

## Q4. The CrySL rule itself

I could not read the rule source. I therefore cannot say, from the source, which method names or receiver types it matches. I also cannot say whether it constrains the parameter list of a matched call, what condition it evaluates, or whether it can match a method that merely shares a name with an SSLContext method. I cannot quote a clause verbatim.

- The repository page states that the repository holds the CrySL rules used in CogniCrypt, and its `JavaCryptographicArchitecture` folder has a `src` directory. https://github.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/tree/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture
- Further checking requires fetching the raw file at the URL given in the task and reading its EVENTS, ORDER, CONSTRAINTS, REQUIRES and ENSURES sections. The exact compiled rule version used by the detector would also be needed.

## Unresolved

- The text of `SSLContext.crysl` as published.
- Whether the detector's rule version matches the file at master.
- The conflict between the Javadoc and the JSSE guide on what a null `KeyManager[]` produces.
- Any official statement of a required or recommended remediation for a `KeyManager[]` not obtained from a KeyManagerFactory.
